pages.reason: Checkpoint state includes optimizer history, RNG, vocabulary mapping and schedule, so a novice needs time to trace save/reload and both equality assertions, distinguish matching predictions from a matching next update, and interpret the saved step-1/five-character CPU output and limited GPU continuation claim.

The two four-token predictions require checking why teacher-forced accuracy is 0.75 while generated accuracy is 0.5 although both exact matches fail, then reconciling loss with open-ended continuations, missing side information and the actual repetitive TinyStories sample.

Reading means following warm-up/no-grad timing code, interpreting 6104 parameters, 24416 FP32 bytes and the actual CPU timing, then separating parameter storage, training memory, attention T×T work, repeated target exposure and the two differently scoped L4 times.

The reader must trace whitespace normalization and the fingerprint equality assertion, interpret three records becoming two contents with 64-character hashes, and consider when code/poem whitespace, duplicate weighting and exact-only deduplication change the meaning of the data.

A novice needs to enumerate character bigrams and follow set intersection/union to the actual 4/8=0.5 result, then distinguish structural overlap from semantic labels and family splitting, including the trigram 3/7 exercise and unimplemented near-duplicate controls.

The four planned CPU records need comparison with the separate measured width-16/32 table; time is needed to distinguish unique documents, update steps and effective targets, work through 2×D×H FLOPs, interpret higher training but lower validation losses with more data, and assess the unmatched target totals and one-seed limit.

The seed-reset code and actual three initialization deviations plus True equality need to be distinguished from quality scores; the reader then compares paired hypothetical A/B differences and thinks through shared seeds, shifted random consumption and the weakness of choosing the luckiest run.

The 90-short/10-long batch requires checking how 90 versus 200 answer positions yield actual 0.3103/0.6897 shares, solving the 180:1 record ratio and separating loss weights from counted tokens, then interpreting the near-doubled supervision in the replay comparison.

The reader distinguishes code points, displayed characters, UTF-8 bytes and tokens using the actual 3/9, 3/3 and 1/4 counts, links length to T×T versus V×D cost, and examines the truncated Chinese-byte generation and replacement character before predicting mixed-text counts.

The reader needs to inspect the two-document BPE diagram, count ab/ba/ac occurrences, trace the Counter and non-overlapping while-loop merge to the actual two-/three-token outputs, and distinguish learned rule order from new-text encoding and held-out tokenizer testing.

The reader follows the ByteLevel BPE setup, full 256-byte alphabet and decode assertion, interprets the actual unusual byte-symbol tokens/13 IDs returning 小鳥🙂new, and connects reversible unseen text to saved tokenizer/model identity and the separate 512-item held-out experiment.

The arithmetic output for three vocabulary sizes is simple, but a novice must balance V×32 embedding/output storage against actual sequence length and rare-token learning, then compare the measured 3894-to-2112 token reduction with parameters rising from 41824 to 57696.

The conditional NLL-to-BPB derivation, seven-byte CPU examples and overlap-window target accounting require careful thought. The personally viewed ranking-reversal figure adds comparison of per-token costs, unequal target counts and common 4193-byte BPB values, with EOS and resource-contract qualifications.

The reader compares the eight printed control IDs with byte IDs shifted by eight, verifies that actual literal <assistant> remains text without ID 4, and thinks through explicit role insertion, BPE special-token handling and why a marker neither selects a role from spelling nor creates model capability.

The seven-byte output lets the reader localize why a single 232 byte displays � while the complete sequence restores 貓🙂. Additional thought distinguishes temporary display from destructive replacement, streaming decode from per-token decode, and the three-/four-byte slice predictions.

The reader traces the three actual shifted windows and their shared boundary tokens, reasons why C inputs need C+1 original IDs and how a short tail breaks the assertion, then separates tokenizer units, document splitting and equal-byte versus equal-token exposure.
